checkpoints: With from+size pagination, each shard must sort its own subset and ship from+size documents to the coordinator, which then merges and sorts again to get the correct global order.
The cost of from+size pagination scales as O(shards × (from+size)) — it grows directly with how deep 'from' goes.
The memory needed for from+size pagination grows linearly with the depth of 'from', since each shard's from+size results must be held before the coordinator can merge them.
The default index.max_result_window = 10000 is not an arbitrary number but a guard rail placed exactly where it should be, stopping the cluster from digging its own grave.

Raising the cap is the wrong instinct because it does not change that cost formula in the slightest — it only removes the safety rail and pushes the cliff further out: today page 900 collapses, raise the cap and page 9000 will collapse instead, the root problem is untouched.

For real-time next-page access, search_after with a stable sort that includes a tie-breaker (usually the primary key) is the right choice: it is a stateless cursor whose cost stays independent of depth, unlike from+size.

For batch-style access such as exporting the whole index or reindexing into a new mapping, scroll or PIT (point-in-time) is the right tool instead, since it holds a fixed snapshot at one moment in time and reads sequentially through the entire set rather than jumping to an arbitrary position.

The "jump straight to page 900" request itself deserves to be questioned: that kind of deep random access is rarely a genuine user need — it's a UX design smell to challenge, not an engineering constraint you should strain to satisfy by breaking the cluster's safety rails.
A per-user Trie is the wrong move — it blows up memory across millions of users and throws away the one thing a Trie is for, a single shared O(k) structure.
The right split is two layers: keep ONE shared global Trie doing candidate generation, the same prefix walk in O(k) for every user.
Re-rank only the small top-K candidate set left after that walk with a per-user signal: finalScore = α·globalFreq + β·userAffinity(word).
The per-user affinity (recent clicks, category weights) lives in a small Redis Hash or ZSET keyed by user, fetched once per request rather than on every keystroke.
Because the per-user signal is fetched once per request instead of on every keystroke, the personalization lookup does not multiply with typing speed.
Because the candidate set left after the prefix walk is already tiny, re-ranking it with that per-user weight is cheap.
The expensive part of the problem — traversing the tree and collecting descendants — stays exactly as shared and as fast as it was before personalization was ever a requirement.

Elasticsearch is near-real-time rather than real-time: a document written via an index call becomes durable immediately, but it only becomes searchable after the next refresh cycle, which by default fires roughly once per second.

Because the index call in question uses the default refresh: false, a search issued immediately afterward races against that periodic refresh cycle instead of against a guaranteed-consistent index state.

The intermittent pass/fail pattern is a timing race, not a deterministic defect in the write path — whether the search lands before or after the refresh has already fired depends on incidental wall-clock delays like network round-trip and test-runner scheduling.

"The write is lost" and "the write is not yet visible to search" are different claims; the document is never dropped or corrupted, so treating this as data loss sends debugging effort toward the wrong root cause.

Setting refresh: "wait_for" on the index call is the correct fix for this read-after-write case: it blocks the write's response until the document becomes searchable by riding the next refresh cycle, without forcing an extra one.
Using refresh: true forces an immediate refresh on every write, which increases I/O cost and interferes with segment merging under load, so it is not a good default for fixing this.

refresh: "wait_for" (or an explicit index refresh) belongs on read-after-write paths like tests or specific user-facing flows, not on every production write, since it still adds latency compared to the default asynchronous refresh: false.
Confirming the fix requires re-running the seed-then-search flow repeatedly rather than trusting a single passing run, since one pass does not prove the race condition is actually closed.

Kafka gives only at-least-once delivery: offsets commit after a message is successfully handled, so a consumer crash or restart resumes from the last committed offset and redelivers messages that were already processed.
A handler that writes to an external store on every message must be idempotent — safe to run again on a message it already applied, without throwing or corrupting state.

`es.create` maps to Elasticsearch's create-only `PUT /_create/<id>` operation, which throws a 409 conflict if a document with that id already exists, so replaying an already-indexed `c`/`u`/`r` message crashes the handler.
`es.delete` throws a 404 when the target id no longer exists, and with no try/catch around the call, replaying an already-processed `d` message also crashes the handler.

`es.index` is a PUT-by-id operation that overwrites whatever document currently holds that id (or creates it if absent), so calling it repeatedly with the same id and payload is a genuinely idempotent upsert, unlike `es.create`.

Folding the three ops `c`/`u`/`r` into a single `es.index({ index, id, document: after })` call, and wrapping `es.delete({ index, id })` in a `.catch(() => undefined)` to swallow 404s, makes the handler safe to reprocess any number of times and converges on the same final document per id.

Diagnosing this kind of bug should start from naming the delivery guarantee that causes redelivery in the first place, then trace down to the two specific non-idempotent calls, before proposing the fix — jumping straight to a code patch skips the actual root cause.

Correctness should be verified by actually replaying already-processed messages (restarting the consumer or resending them) and confirming no exception is thrown and each id ends up with exactly one document holding the latest data, with no duplicates.
Debezium's default `decimal.handling.mode` is "precise", which serializes a NUMERIC column like `price` as a base64-encoded VariableScaleDecimal struct rather than a plain number.

An Elasticsearch mapping that declares that field as `double` either rejects a base64-encoded VariableScaleDecimal outright, or, with dynamic mapping enabled, indexes it as an opaque string — either way the price data is corrupted or unusable, and nothing throws an exception to signal the failure.

Setting `decimal.handling.mode: double` on the connector config fixes the serialization by emitting a real IEEE double instead of the base64 form, at the cost of a small precision loss versus `precise` — an acceptable trade-off since a search index is not the system of record for money.
A PostgreSQL replication slot is a server-side bookmark holding every WAL segment not yet acknowledged by the consumer, and it does not expire or self-clean on its own.

If the CDC consumer is down for an extended period, the un-drained slot causes WAL to accumulate without bound on the PostgreSQL disk, which can eventually fill the disk and take down the entire database, not just the CDC pipeline.

Guarding against this requires alerting on the lag between `pg_replication_slots.confirmed_flush_lsn` and `pg_current_wal_lsn`, plus setting `max_slot_wal_keep_size` (PostgreSQL 13+) so the slot self-invalidates and forces a resync instead of growing unbounded.

Leaving a table at PostgreSQL's default REPLICA IDENTITY means a DELETE event's `before` image contains only the primary key; any consumer that needs the full old row, such as an audit log, will silently receive nulls for every other column unless the table is switched to REPLICA IDENTITY FULL.

The decimal-handling defect is actively corrupting data right now and should block the merge, while the replication-slot risk is a latent production outage that must ship with monitoring rather than as a follow-up ticket; approval should be conditioned on concrete evidence — a decimal price inserted and confirmed as a correct number in Elasticsearch, plus a stopped-consumer test confirming the slot-lag alert actually fires.
Reasons from the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) — a standard every Debian package follows — instead of scanning the whole disk with find/locate, grounding confidence in that reproducibility.
Knows system config lives under /etc, so nginx config is at /etc/nginx/, with the main file nginx.conf and sites under conf.d/ and sites-enabled/.
Knows runtime/log data lives under /var, so nginx logs are at /var/log/nginx/access.log and error.log.
Verifies via the package manager: dpkg -L nginx | grep -E 'etc|log' lists every installed nginx file and where it went.
Verifies via the running process: nginx -T dumps the config actually in use along with each file's path.
Confirms the service's binary path: systemctl cat nginx shows the ExecStart path.
Confirms nginx is actually listening: ss -tlnp shows it bound to a port.
Line one `-rw-r--r--` (644): owner alice has read+write but no execute on `deploy.sh`; group and other have read-only.
The missing execute bit on `deploy.sh` is the first, independent cause of `permission denied`; fix it with `chmod u+x deploy.sh` (or `chmod 750`).

Line two `dr--r--r--` (444) is the permission on directory `/opt/app` itself, not the script — and on a directory the `x` bit doesn't mean "execute" but "traverse": the right to enter the directory to resolve a path to files inside it.

The directory has `r` (names can be listed) but lacks `x`, so the kernel blocks even reaching `deploy.sh` inside it; this is the second, independent cause — fix it with `chmod u+x /opt/app` (or `chmod 750`).
`chmod 777` opens `rwxrwxrwx` to every user on the system, letting any user or process overwrite the script — breaking integrity.
`chmod 777` also lets any user read secrets or credentials embedded in the script — breaking confidentiality.
This is a mistake because it violates the Principle of Least Privilege: only the minimum permissions needed should be granted — `750` on the script and `750` on the directory, not `777`.
Verify the fix by re-running `ls -l`/`ls -ld` to confirm the `x` bit now appears on both, then running `sudo -u alice ./deploy.sh` to confirm the script actually runs.

The inode is the single foundational concept explaining both phenomena: it is the structure holding a file's metadata (size, permissions, owner, timestamps) and pointers to its data blocks, while the filename is merely a directory entry mapping a name to an inode number — the name does not live in the inode.

Within the same filesystem, `mv` only rewrites the directory entry to remap the name to the existing inode, leaving the inode and its data blocks untouched, so it is nearly instant regardless of file size.
`cp` instead allocates a new inode and copies every data block to it, so its cost is proportional to file size, explaining why copying a 10GB file takes noticeably longer than moving it.

The 'df shows free space but writes fail' paradox happens because blocks and inodes are counted as separate, independently-exhaustible capacity pools — e.g. millions of tiny files can consume the entire inode table while data blocks remain free, so `df` shows space available yet `df -i` shows 0 free inodes and new files cannot be created.

Another scenario is a file that was `rm`'d while a process still holds it open: the inode's reference count stays above zero, so the kernel does not free the data blocks, and the space vanishes with no filename pointing to it.
To investigate on production, first run both `df -h` and `df -i` to determine whether it is blocks or inodes that are exhausted.

If blocks are full but `ls`/`du` show no large file, use `lsof | grep deleted` (or `lsof +L1`) to find the process holding the deleted-but-open file, then restart it or `truncate` it to reclaim the blocks.
Use `du -xh --max-depth=1 /` to localize which directory is consuming the space.
First command: run `systemctl status myworker` and read the Active state, Main PID, `code=`/`signal=` fields, and the last log lines shown inline.
Follow-up command: run `journalctl -u myworker -n 50 --no-pager` to see the output right before the process died.

Interpret `active (exited)`: the main process exited immediately with `status=0/SUCCESS`, and under the default `Type=simple` systemd reads that as "ran and exited successfully," not as still running.

Hypothesis from `active (exited)`: the unit's `Type` is misconfigured — a daemonizing (double-forking) service needs `Type=forking` + `PIDFile`, while a foreground worker must stay in the foreground for `Type=simple` to track it correctly.
Interpret 137 as 128 + 9 = SIGKILL — the process was hard-killed rather than exiting on its own (SIGKILL cannot be trapped or handled).
Hypothesis from 137: the OOM killer is the prime suspect (RAM fills up and the kernel selects this process to kill), distinguished from 143 = 128 + 15 (SIGTERM, graceful shutdown).
Confirm the OOM hypothesis with `dmesg | grep -i oom` or `journalctl -k | grep oom-killer`, and check the unit's `MemoryMax`/cgroup limit.

Synthesize the full cycle: start → main process exits 0 (active exited) → `Restart` brings it back → the next run gets OOM-killed with 137 → repeat — i.e. a misconfigured `Type` combined with memory pressure, not random flakiness.

Identifies the fork-storm as the primary cause of slowness: spawning a separate grep process per file via `for f in $(cat files.txt); do grep ...; done` costs thousands of fork()/execve() calls, and that process-spawn overhead — not the log scanning itself — is what eats most of the 20 minutes.

Identifies the two temp files (/tmp/files.txt, /tmp/hits.txt) as an anti-pattern: they serialize the pipeline (write fully, then read back) and waste disk IO, instead of letting data flow straight through a kernel pipe with the stages running in parallel.

Flags the unquoted `$(cat files.txt)` word-splitting bug as a distinct correctness issue: iterating over the unquoted command substitution breaks on filenames containing spaces (or other IFS characters).
Flags the redundant no-op stages as anti-patterns: `cat hits.txt | awk '{print}'` is a useless-use-of-cat feeding an awk that transforms nothing, and `sort | uniq` should simply be `sort -u`.
Rewrites the script as a much shorter single pipeline, e.g. `grep -rl 'ERROR' /var/log/app --include='*.log' | sort -u` (or equivalently `find /var/log/app -name '*.log' -exec grep -l 'ERROR' {} +`).

Explains the mechanism by which the rewrite eliminates the fork-storm: `grep -r` (or `-exec {} +`) passes many files to a single grep invocation instead of spawning one per file, and `-exec {} +` self-batches by ARG_MAX so it stays safe even with tens of thousands of files.

Explains why the rewrite handles a huge directory without blowing up RAM: grep streams line by line holding only the current file in its buffer, and there's no `$(cat)` loading the whole file list into shell memory and no temp files, so memory stays near-constant regardless of directory size.
Proposes a verification step: benchmark both versions with `time`, and test a filename containing a space to prove the rewritten version doesn't word-split.
